records.place: Malpica de Tajo, Dominio de Valdepusa, Toledo, Castilla-La Mancha

wine.name: Emeritus
wine.classification: Vino de Pago, a single estate Denominación de Origen, recognised in 2002
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon leads, with Syrah and Petit Verdot in shares that move widely with the vintage.
wine.sites: The Dominio de Valdepusa beside the Tajo at Malpica, west of Toledo: the Cabernet Sauvignon planted from 1974 and the Syrah and Petit Verdot added later, all of it under drip irrigation on a dry site.
wine.making: After fermentation the wine is aged in French oak barrels for well over a year, two years by several merchants' sheets, before it is bottled. It is assembled from the estate's own grapes alone, as the rules of its appellation require.
wine.glass: Deep cherry red; plum jam and wild berries on an intense, clean nose; round and powerful in the mouth, with a firm, fine frame of tannin and a long finish led by ripe fruit.
wine.ageing: Firm and dense on release, it gains from several years in bottle and keeps for well over a decade in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The wine's name in Roman lettering, Emeritus, the Latin for one who has served out his time.
The estate's own appellation, granted to this single estate alone, not DO La Mancha.
Spain's rank for a single estate with a Denominación de Origen of its own.

records.table: Emeritus is the estate red of Marqués de Griñón at the Dominio de Valdepusa, west of Toledo, a single estate with an appellation of its own. Cabernet Sauvignon led, with Syrah and Petit Verdot and long ageing in French oak, it is dense and firm: decant it.
records.story: By the family's account the Dominio de Valdepusa, beside the Tajo at Malpica west of Toledo, has been in its hands since 1292. Carlos Falcó (1937 to 2020), Marqués de Griñón, inherited it from his grandfather and studied agronomy at the Catholic University of Louvain, finishing in 1959. In 1974 he planted Cabernet Sauvignon there, a Bordeaux grape on a plateau of Airén and Cencibel, and watered it by drip irrigation, then a novelty in Spain's vineyards; the first commercial wine came from the 1982 harvest. Syrah and Petit Verdot followed. On 19 July 2002 the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha recognised Dominio de Valdepusa as a Denominación de Origen of its own, a Vino de Pago; the family holds it to be the first single estate appellation of Spain, and the Spanish ministry of agriculture ratified its rules in February 2003. Emeritus, the estate's Cabernet led blend with Syrah and Petit Verdot, is the wine of that work. Falcó died in Madrid in March 2020, of Covid. For a sommelier Emeritus is where the study of the Vinos de Pago begins: Bordeaux grapes on the plateau south of Madrid, with an appellation for one estate alone.

others.name: Marqués de Griñón Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The estate's first wine, from the Cabernet planted in 1974 and first sold from the 1982 harvest.

traps: Emeritus carries the Dominio de Valdepusa appellation, a Vino de Pago of its own, never DO La Mancha, though the estate lies in Castilla-La Mancha.
Wines labelled Marqués de Griñón Rioja come from Rioja, not from Valdepusa; only the estate's own wines carry the Dominio de Valdepusa appellation.
The label spells the name EMERITVS, with the Roman V for U: it is the same wine as Emeritus.

cards.front: Marqués de Griñón at Valdepusa: what was planted in 1974, and how was it watered?

report: Searches for this record: 11 of the group's share of 35; no fetch tried. The house's own pages (marquesdegrinon.com, grandespagos.com) gave 1292, 1974 and the claim of the first Vino de Pago with the European Union in 2003, hedged as the family's account; Wikipedia's list dates Finca Élez with Valdepusa, so the first is the family's claim and no more. The Petit Verdot as a pioneer planting in Spain rests on Grandes Pagos alone and is left out.

The plan's note is answered: the BOE notice of 2009 cites the Orden de 19 de julio de 2002 (DOCM of 7 August 2002) that recognised the Denominación de Origen Dominio de Valdepusa, so the classification says 2002; Wikipedia and its mirrors give 2003, which the family's site explains as the European recognition.

Carlos Falcó's dates (Seville, 3 February 1937, to Madrid, 20 March 2020) are the Real Academia de la Historia's, with wein.plus's obituary (died of Covid at 83) as the second; Louvain and 1959 rest on the Academia alone with the family's site, and the year he inherited (1955 by one obituary, 1957 by the Academia) is left out.

The blend rests on two vintages' sheets (about 55 per cent Cabernet, 25 to 32 Petit Verdot, 12 to 20 Syrah); the two years in oak on Vinos Cutanda (24 months, French oak, steel for both fermentations) and espagne-gourmet.com (24 to 26 months in oak). No house sheet for Emeritus was found, nor its first vintage (merchants list 2002 and 2003; a Delectable page shows 1997), so neither is taught.

The drip irrigation of 1974 rests on the Ministry of Agriculture's Vida Rural of 1995 and Decanter; the year Falcó saw it in Israel conflicts in Decanter's own pages (1972 against the early 1980s) and is left out, as are Emile Peynaud's advice and every consultant who may be living.
No soil is taught for Valdepusa: no source read named it. The founding year is left empty: the family's 1292 is a claim of possession, and 1974 is the first planting, not a founding.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not on the region record's producers line. No swap proposed; no living member of the family is named.

records.place: Valdepeñas, DO Valdepeñas, Ciudad Real, Castilla-La Mancha

wine.name: Viña Albali Gran Reserva
wine.classification: Gran Reserva, the Spanish ageing category of at least five years, eighteen months in oak
wine.grapes: Tempranillo alone, known in Valdepeñas and across La Mancha as Cencibel.
wine.sites: Tempranillo of the Valdepeñas appellation, the high, dry plain around the town in the south of Ciudad Real, beside the wider La Mancha.
wine.making: Fermented at a controlled 26 to 28 degrees Celsius, the wine is aged for at least eighteen months in American oak barrels and then for three to six years in bottle before it is released.
wine.glass: Deep ruby with amber at the rim; ripe cherry, leather and green pepper over the sweet vanilla of American oak; round and balanced in the mouth, with tannin softened by its long ageing.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink after its long rest in barrel and bottle, it keeps for some years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; open it half an hour ahead, or decant it gently off any sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: A red aged at least five years in all, at least eighteen months of them in oak casks.
The town's own Denominación de Origen, separate from DO La Mancha, its rules approved in 1968.
The house's brand, dated by the company to 1962, when it bottled its wine in Madrid.

records.table: Viña Albali Gran Reserva is Félix Solís's long aged Tempranillo from Valdepeñas, the separate appellation in the south of La Mancha: at least eighteen months in American oak and years in bottle before release, it comes ready to drink, with leather and soft tannin.
records.story: In 1952 the founder and his wife left Villanueva de los Infantes for Valdepeñas, where, by the company's history, they bought the Casa del Huerto del Cura and began to make wine there. In 1962, by the same history, the founder bought a bottling plant in Madrid, whose bars and restaurants had been taking his wine, brought up in casks and bottled by hand; the brand Viña Albali dates from that year. The Valdepeñas appellation had its rules approved by a ministerial order of August 1968, and after it the bottling moved home to the town. The firm grew from a family winery into a group trading as Félix Solís Avantis, with cellars beyond Valdepeñas, and Viña Albali became its name in shops at home and abroad. The Gran Reserva carries Spain's ageing category of Gran Reserva to a wide public: Tempranillo held at least eighteen months in American oak and years more in bottle, released when it is ready to drink. For a sommelier it is the plain lesson of the ageing terms on a Spanish label, and a reminder that Valdepeñas is an appellation of its own, not La Mancha.

others.name: Viña Albali Reserva
others.note: The step below the Gran Reserva in the same Valdepeñas line, with vanilla and jam on the nose.

others.name: Viña Albali Gran Reserva de Familia
others.note: Tempranillo with a share of Cabernet Sauvignon, about two years in American oak by the house's account.

Gran Reserva is an ageing category, not a vineyard or a selection of grapes: it rests on years in oak and in bottle.
Viña Albali is the brand; the house is Félix Solís, trading as Félix Solís Avantis.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35; no fetch tried. The plan's note is answered: the house trades as Félix Solís Avantis, 1952 is on its own company page and history and on Brands of Spain's member page, and the label reads Viña Albali Gran Reserva, DO Valdepeñas.
The founder and his wife are named on the house's own pages, but their dates were found in no source, so they are described; the founder's son, who leads the firm, is living and is not named.

The house's history puts the move of the bottling to Valdepeñas in 1968 in one place and 1972 in another, so the story says after the order of 1968; the 1968 order (BOE of 14 September 1968) is the Valdepeñas regulation, not the first naming of the appellation, which the record does not date.

The making, the glass and the food come from the house's own Gran Reserva sheet (vinaalbali.com and felixsolisavantis.com agree); the sheet's page address names the wine Selección Privada, which the record does not teach as a label term for want of sight of the bottle.
The house's sheet advises 18 to 20 degrees Celsius; the record keeps the Codex's 15 to 17 for a medium red.

The region record's producers line calls Viña Albali the cheap aged Cencibel that taught the world Reserva and Gran Reserva; the flagship record carries no price, and that line's cheap is a word the Flagships tab would refuse.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. No swap proposed.

records.place: Villarrobledo, DO La Mancha, Albacete, Castilla-La Mancha

wine.name: Estola Reserva
wine.classification: Reserva, an ageing category of Spanish wine law
wine.grapes: Tempranillo, the Cencibel of La Mancha, blended with Cabernet Sauvignon.
wine.sites: Grapes of the La Mancha plateau around Villarrobledo, in the province of Albacete, on the dry plain where the house has made wine since 1947.
wine.making: After fermentation the wine is aged in American oak barrels, for twenty four months by the house's current sheet, and then rests in bottle in the house's cellars before release. By its own account the house laid down its first cellar of Bordeaux style oak barrels in 1961.
wine.glass: Cherry red with a brick rim; plum, liquorice and the sweet clove and vanilla of American oak on a warm, intense nose; full and round in the mouth, balsamic, with the fruit and the wood in balance.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release after its two years in oak and its rest in bottle, it keeps well for some years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass, with roast lamb or game.

label.means: The house's brand for its aged and young wines, first used for the 1965 vintage.
Spanish law's ageing category: a red aged at least three years before release, at least one of them in oak.
The appellation of the plateau, its first rules approved by ministerial order in 1976.

records.table: Estola Reserva is Bodegas Ayuso's aged red from Villarrobledo, in the Albacete corner of La Mancha: Tempranillo with Cabernet Sauvignon, aged in American oak. By the house's account its 1965 was the first Reserva of La Mancha; pour it with roast lamb.
records.story: The founder set up his own winery at Villarrobledo, in the province of Albacete, in 1947, when the plateau's wine was sold mostly in bulk. In 1961, by the house's account, he fitted out cellars with Bordeaux style oak barrels, the first ageing cellar of the region, and began to sell his wine in bottle. With the 1965 vintage came Estola, a red aged in oak that the house holds to be the first Reserva of La Mancha. The denomination itself, first named in 1932, was taken up again only in 1973 and given its first rules by ministerial order in 1976, so Estola came before the rules that govern it. The brand grew into a whole range, from young wines to a Gran Reserva held three years in oak, and the Reserva, Tempranillo blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and aged in American oak, two years by the house's sheet, became the bottle the house is known by. For a sommelier Estola Reserva shows how La Mancha learnt to age its reds: a plateau of bulk wine that turned, cellar by cellar, to barrels and to the words Reserva and Gran Reserva on the label.

others.name: Estola Gran Reserva
others.note: The long aged red of the range, thirty six months in oak by the house's sheet.

others.name: Estola Crianza
others.note: The younger aged red, twelve months in American oak barrels.

traps: Estola is the brand and Ayuso the house: the bottle reads Estola, and the range runs from young wines to a Gran Reserva.
The claim that the 1965 Estola was the first Reserva of La Mancha is the house's own, made for a wine older than the denomination's rules of 1976.
Bodegas Ayuso is at Villarrobledo in Albacete, not in Valdepeñas or Tomelloso in Ciudad Real.

cards.back: 1965; the house holds it to be the first Reserva of La Mancha.

cards.front: How long does Estola Reserva spend in barrel, and in what oak?
cards.back: Two years in American oak barrels, by the house's current sheet.

questions.q: A guest asks what gives Bodegas Ayuso's Estola Reserva its sweet spice and vanilla. Which answer fits?
opts: Ageing in American oak barrels
Fermentation in new French oak vats
A long rest on its lees in clay jars
Grapes dried on mats after harvest
questions.exp: The Reserva is aged in American oak, two years by the house's sheet, and its vanilla and sweet spice show in the glass; it is not fermented in new French oak vats.

questions.q: Bodegas Ayuso holds that its Estola of one vintage was the first Reserva of La Mancha. Which vintage?
questions.exp: Estola began with the 1965 vintage; 1947 is the year the house was founded and 1976 the year the denomination's first rules were approved.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's share of 35, with one more shared with Virgen de las Viñas on the denomination's history; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1947, 1961 and 1965 stand on the house's catalogues in four languages, the regional tourism body's page and the London Wine Competition's profile; a BOE order of 1983 (8 September) names the founder's firm at Villarrobledo, and the founder's own dates were found nowhere, so he is described, not named.

The first Reserva of La Mancha and the first ageing cellar of the region are the house's claims, hedged; note that the Consejo Regulador was formed in 1973 or 1974 (the DO's own pages differ) and the first rules came in 1976, so the Estola of 1965 was a Reserva before the denomination's Reserva existed.

The blend is given as Tempranillo and Cabernet Sauvignon without shares: no sheet read gave them. The twenty four months in American oak are on the house's product page and its 2024 catalogue; the glass is the house's note, with the plum and liquorice of a critic's tasting quoted on its site, the critic living and not named.
The house advises about 18 degrees Celsius, inside the Codex's 16 to 18 for a full red. Its new winery of 2018 rests on one directory and is left out.
The region record's producers line calls Estola Reserva the best known aged red of DO La Mancha; the record says only the bottle the house is known by.

wine.name: Tomillar Airén
wine.grapes: Airén alone, the traditional white grape of the La Mancha plateau.
wine.sites: Airén from the members' vineyards around Tomelloso, in the middle of the La Mancha plain in the province of Ciudad Real.
wine.making: A young white, a joven of the denomination: by the merchants' sheets the grapes are lightly crushed and given a short, cold maceration on their skins in closed tanks under carbon dioxide, then fermented at a low temperature, and the wine is bottled young without any time in oak, to be drunk within the year of its harvest.
wine.glass: Pale straw with green glints; ripe banana, apple and grapefruit on the nose; light in body and dry, with soft acidity, a faint prickle and a short, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young, within the year after the harvest, while its fruit is fresh; it does not gain from keeping.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass, with Manchego cheese or a plate of fried fish.

label.means: The co-operative's long standing brand for its wines, young and aged.
The grape, La Mancha's traditional white, named alone on the label.
The appellation of the plateau across Albacete, Ciudad Real, Cuenca and Toledo.

records.table: Tomillar Airén is the young white of Virgen de las Viñas, the growers' co-operative of Tomelloso: Airén alone, fermented cool and bottled without oak. Pour it cold and young, a glass of the grape the La Mancha plateau was built on.
records.story: Virgen de las Viñas was founded in Tomelloso in 1961 by a small group of the town's growers, who pooled their grapes in a co-operative named for the Virgin of the Vineyards. Tomelloso lies in the middle of the La Mancha plain, in the province of Ciudad Real, and Airén, the plateau's traditional white grape, was the town's living: the vine stands up to drought and gives a mild wine of soft acidity. The co-operative grew quickly as more of the town's growers joined it, and it later added an olive mill, so that it trades as a bodega and almazara. Its wines are sold under the Tomillar name within the La Mancha denomination, from young whites of Airén to aged reds of Tempranillo and Cabernet Sauvignon. The co-operative also runs a cultural contest that bears its name, and since 2011 the prize works have hung in a museum of contemporary art beside its winery. Tomillar Airén is the plainest glass it makes and the one a sommelier should taste: Airén alone, fermented cool and bottled young, the grape the plain was built on.

others.name: Tomillar Reserva
others.note: The co-operative's aged red under the same brand, Tempranillo with Cabernet Sauvignon, a Reserva of DO La Mancha.

traps: Virgen de las Viñas is a growers' co-operative, not a family estate: the grapes come from its members' vineyards around Tomelloso.
Airén's mild, soft style is the grape's nature, not a fault: a young Airén is made for freshness, not for keeping.

cards.front: Virgen de las Viñas: what kind of producer is it, and where?
cards.back: A growers' co-operative at Tomelloso in Ciudad Real, founded in 1961.

cards.front: What does Tomillar Airén show of La Mancha's traditional white grape?
cards.back: Airén alone, young and unoaked: pale, light and soft, with banana, apple and pear, to be drunk within the year.

questions.q: A guest asks how the Tomillar Airén of Virgen de las Viñas is made. Which answer fits?

Aged two years in American oak barrels
Fermented on its skins like an orange wine
Aged under flor in a solera of old casks
questions.exp: It is a joven: fermented at a controlled low temperature and bottled young without oak, to keep Airén's fresh fruit; two years in American oak is the way of an aged red.

questions.q: Virgen de las Viñas, the Tomelloso winery behind Tomillar Airén, dates from 1961. What sort of winery is it?
opts: A co-operative of the town's growers
A noble family's single estate
A merchant house bottling in Madrid
A Vino de Pago of one estate
questions.exp: The town's growers pooled their grapes in 1961 in a co-operative named for the Virgin of the Vineyards; a single estate Vino de Pago, like Dominio de Valdepusa, is another thing.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35, with one more shared with Bodegas Ayuso; no fetch tried, and no site of the co-operative's own was found by search, so no technical sheet of Tomillar Airén was read.

The plan's note is answered in part: 1961 stands on the regional tourism body and the Sommeliers Choice Awards' profile, which differ on the founders (17 and 15), so the story says a small group of growers. The wine is attested by FENAVIN's Premios Airén por el Mundo, which entered a Tomillar in its young Airén class; the label words Tomillar Airén and DO La Mancha are not confirmed from the bottle.

With no sheet, the making, the glass and the ageing follow the DO La Mancha's own pages on young Airén (no barrel, cool controlled fermentation, drunk within the year; banana, apple and pear, pale with green glints, soft acidity); the checker should look for the co-operative's sheet. The night harvest the Consejo reported at the co-operative concerned Chardonnay and is left out.

The merger with Vinícola de Tomelloso and San José presented on 2 March 2026 (Vinetur, Forbes España) is left out, as the note asks: it is recent and the co-operative's name may change with it, which the integrator should watch.
The museum's year (2001) rests on one source and is left out; the co-operative's president, named in a harvest report, is living and is not named.
The region record's producers line calls it one of the largest wineries in Europe; the record does not rank it.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. No swap proposed, though the pick is thin: a co-operative's young white, chosen under the thin region rule, and said to be so.

records.place: Retuerta del Bullaque, Montes de Toledo, Ciudad Real, Castilla-La Mancha

wine.name: Dehesa del Carrizal Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.classification: Vino de Pago, a single estate Denominación de Origen, recognised in 2006
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the variety the estate was first planted with in 1987.
wine.sites: The estate's first vines, Cabernet Sauvignon planted from 1987 at 800 to 900 metres in the Montes de Toledo near the Cabañeros National Park, on raña: slopes at the foot of the hills, of clay strewn with quartzite cobbles over acid soils.
wine.making: Fermented and then aged for twelve to fifteen months in French oak barrels, a mix of new casks and casks up to four years old, the time moving with the vintage by the estate's own sheets.
wine.glass: Blackberry, blueberry and clove with bay leaf, chocolate and a balsamic note; smooth in the mouth yet powerful, with ripe tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to open within a few years of the vintage, it holds and grows more savoury for several years beyond in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; open it ahead or decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's name and its own appellation, recognised by Castilla-La Mancha in 2006.
Spain's rank for a single estate with a Denominación de Origen of its own.
The variety named on the label, the estate's first planting.

records.table: Dehesa del Carrizal Cabernet Sauvignon comes from a single estate in the Montes de Toledo with an appellation of its own: vines planted from 1987 at 800 to 900 metres, aged a year and more in French oak. Balsamic and smooth, with ripe tannin, it wants an hour's air.
records.story: Dehesa del Carrizal lies at Retuerta del Bullaque, in the Montes de Toledo north of Ciudad Real, beside the Cabañeros National Park, in hill country that, by the estate's account, had no tradition of wine. In 1987 a doctor and businessman who had bought the hunting estate planted Cabernet Sauvignon there, a Bordeaux grape far from the plateau's Airén and Cencibel, and the first wine, a Cabernet Sauvignon, came from the 1989 harvest. Syrah came at the end of the 1990s, and Merlot, Tempranillo, Chardonnay and Petit Verdot joined them on raña, the local name for slopes and plains of eroded clay strewn with quartzite cobbles, at 800 to 900 metres, where hot days and cold nights ripen the grapes slowly. By an order of 1 February 2006 the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha recognised the estate as a Vino de Pago, a Denominación de Origen for one estate alone. In 2010 it passed to another family. The Cabernet Sauvignon is the wine the estate was built on, and the Colección Privada, blended only in chosen years, stands above it. For a sommelier it is a plain lesson of the plateau's pagos: a hill estate outside the old appellations that won a name of its own with a Bordeaux grape.

others.name: Colección Privada
others.note: The estate's selection, a blend of Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petit Verdot and Tempranillo in new French oak, made only in chosen years.

others.name: Dehesa del Carrizal Syrah
others.note: The estate's Syrah, from vines planted at the end of the 1990s.

others.note: The estate's white, from the same hill vineyards.

traps: Dehesa del Carrizal is its own Vino de Pago, not DO La Mancha and not Dominio de Valdepusa, which is another single estate appellation of the region.
The Cabernet Sauvignon is the estate's founding wine; Colección Privada is the blend it makes only in chosen years.

cards.front: Dehesa del Carrizal: in what year was it made a Vino de Pago, and by whom?
cards.back: In 2006, by an order of the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha.

cards.front: What is raña, the ground of Dehesa del Carrizal's vineyards?
cards.back: The local name for eroded slopes and plains of clay strewn with quartzite cobbles, at 800 to 900 metres in the Montes de Toledo.

questions.q: A guest asks what kind of ground the Dehesa del Carrizal Cabernet Sauvignon grows on. Which answer fits?
opts: Raña, clay with quartzite cobbles at altitude
Deep gravel beside a tidal estuary
Volcanic ash on the slopes of a cone
Chalk on a low plain by the sea
questions.exp: The estate's vines grow on raña at 800 to 900 metres in the Montes de Toledo; deep gravel beside an estuary is the ground of the Médoc, not of the hills of Ciudad Real.

questions.q: Dehesa del Carrizal was founded in 1987 in the Montes de Toledo. What rank did the regional government give it in 2006?
opts: Vino de Pago, for one estate alone
Denominación de Origen Calificada
Vino de la Tierra de Castilla
Vino de Calidad with a geographical name
questions.exp: An order of 1 February 2006 made it a Vino de Pago, an appellation for one estate; Calificada is a rank for a whole region, such as Rioja or Priorat, never for one estate.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's share of 35; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: the Vino de Pago rests on the Orden de 1 de febrero de 2006 (cited in the BOE of 11 May 2007) and the estate's own page; 1987 and the first Cabernet of 1989 are the estate's, with Wikipedia and the wein.plus glossary for 1987; the Cabernet Sauvignon is made under that name, and Colección Privada, made only in chosen years, is the house's selection above it, so the pick stands with Colección Privada taught first among the others.

The founder is named on the estate's page and in Wikipedia; his dates were found nowhere, so he is described as the page describes him, a doctor and businessman. The family that took the estate in 2010 is not named, as its members are living.
The plan's why calls it a hunting estate; no source read says so, and the record leaves it out.

The estate's sheets differ on the barrel time (12 to 14 months in the Spanish sheet, 15 in the English), hence twelve to fifteen months; the vines' age (over 25 or over 35 years) is left out as volatile. 800 metres and the raña rest on Grandes Pagos de España and the estate's page.

The glass joins the estate's own note (balsamic, smooth yet powerful, long) to the Guía de Vinos Gourmets' note of the 2013 that the estate published (blackberry, blueberry, clove, bay leaf, chocolate); the estate advises 15 to 17 degrees Celsius, as the record does.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. No swap proposed.
